entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The 'Plan-Do-Check-Adjust' (PDCA) cycle, developed in the early 20th century, is an iterative four-step management method that has profoundly influenced modern business practices and quality management. Originating from the works of W. Edwards Deming, an American statistician, the PDCA cycle encapsulates a systematic approach to problem-solving and continuous improvement. This method gained prominence in the post-World War II era, particularly in Japan's industrial sectors, where it was instrumental in the country's rapid economic recovery and quality enhancement. The cycle's global adoption exemplifies its significance in shaping management philosophies and practices across various sectors worldwide.

The PDCA cycle consists of four distinct phases: Plan, Do, Check, and Adjust. Initially, organizations identify a problem and develop a plan for improvement. Following this, the plan is implemented on a small scale (the 'Do' phase), which allows for testing and evaluation. The effectiveness of the implementation is then assessed during the 'Check' phase, leading to adjustments and refinements in the process during the 'Adjust' stage. This cyclical process not only fosters an environment of continuous improvement but has also been pivotal in the development of methodologies such as Total Quality Management (TQM) and Six Sigma, which have transformed industries by significantly reducing waste and enhancing product quality.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA, also known as the Deming cycle, Shewhart cycle, or PDSA — Plan-Do-Study-Act in W. Edwards Deming's preferred formulation) is a four-stage iterative management methodology for continuous improvement of processes, products, and services — one of the foundational frameworks of quality management, lean manufacturing, and organisational improvement. The cycle consists of four stages: Plan (identify an opportunity for improvement and plan a change), Do (implement the change on a small scale), Check/Study (analyse the results and determine whether the change achieved the desired improvement), and Act/Adjust (if the improvement was successful, implement it on a larger scale; if not, revise the plan and repeat the cycle). The methodology is designed to be iterative — the 'Act' stage feeds back into the 'Plan' stage of the next cycle — creating a continuous spiral of learning and improvement.

The PDCA cycle was developed by Walter A. Shewhart (1891–1967) — the American physicist and statistician who pioneered statistical process control at Bell Telephone Laboratories — and was popularised and elaborated by W. Edwards Deming (1900–1993), who introduced it to Japanese industry during the post-war reconstruction period (from 1950 onwards).
